# Data Visualization

A chart is **read by people and executed by you**. This skill turns "make it look
good" into a procedure with checks, so the result is right by construction rather
than by taste.

**The method here is design-system-agnostic.** Nothing in the procedure, the form
heuristic, the six checks, or the mark specs is specific to one product. A design
system supplies a small set of *parameters* (its ramps, a categorical order, a
diverging pair, a status palette, a texture, its surfaces, its filter components);
the method consumes them unchanged. A **validated default palette** is the
reference instance, fully specified in `references/palette.md`. To target your
brand, read that file's structure and substitute its values - touch nothing else.

> The single most important habit: **the color part is computable, so compute it.**
> Never eyeball whether a palette is colorblind-safe - run `scripts/validate_palette.js`.

## The procedure - do these in order

Color comes LAST. Most bad charts pick colors first.

1. **Pick the form.** What is the data's job - magnitude, identity, polarity, a
   single headline, change-over-time? The job picks the chart type, and sometimes
   the answer is *not a chart* (a stat tile or hero number). -> `references/choosing-a-form.md`
2. **Assign color by the job it does.** Categorical (identity), sequential
   (magnitude), diverging (polarity), or status (state) - each has one rule.
   Assign categorical hues in fixed order, never cycled. -> `references/color-formula.md`
3. **VALIDATE the palette - run the script, don't reason about Delta E.**
   `node scripts/validate_palette.js "<hex,hex,...>" --mode light` (relative to
   this skill's base directory - or load it as `<script type="module">` in the
   chart's own page, where it reads
   `data-palette` off `<body>` and logs a `console.table` report). It returns
   pass/fail on the lightness band, chroma floor, adjacent-pair CVD separation,
   the normal-vision floor, and contrast. Fix anything that FAILs before continuing. Re-run for
   `--mode dark` with that mode's surface.
4. **Apply mark specs & spacers.** Thin marks, 4px rounded data-ends anchored to
   the baseline, 2px lines, >=8px markers, a 2px surface gap between fills (stacked
   segments and adjacent bars alike) and a 2px surface ring on overlapping marks,
   selective direct labels. -> `references/marks-and-anatomy.md`
5. **Add the hover layer - by default.** An HTML/SVG chart *is* interactive; ship
   a crosshair+tooltip on line/area and a per-mark hover tooltip on bar/dot/cell.
   The only form that skips it is a bare stat tile with no plot. Hit targets bigger
   than the mark; filters in one row above the charts. -> `references/interaction.md`
6. **Final accessibility pass.** For >= 2 series a legend is always present and <= 4
   are also direct-labeled (a single series needs no legend box - the title names
   it), so identity is never color-alone; a table view exists; dark mode is **selected** - its own
   steps from the same ramps, validated against the dark surface, not an automatic
   flip; texture is available for the CVD/print/forced-colors case.
7. **Render it and look at it.** The validator checks color, not layout - open or
   screenshot the output and eyeball it for label collisions, geometry, and overflow
   before calling it done.

Then check the result against **`references/anti-patterns.md`** - it is the catalog
of what goes wrong. If your chart matches an entry, it's wrong.

## Non-negotiables (true in every design system)

- **Assign categorical hues in fixed order, never cycled.** A 9th series is never a
  generated hue - it folds into "Other," small multiples, or composite encoding.
- **One axis.** Never a dual-axis chart (two y-scales). Two measures of different
  scale -> two charts, small multiples, or indexed to a common base. *(This is the
  #1 chart mistake - see anti-patterns.)*
- **Color follows the entity, never its rank.** A filter that changes the series
  count must not repaint the survivors.
- **Sequential = one hue, light->dark. Diverging = two hues + a neutral gray
  midpoint.** Never a rainbow; never a hue at the diverging midpoint.
- **Run the validator before shipping any categorical palette.** CVD Delta E >= 8 is the
  target (OKLab ×100); 6-8 is a floor that is legal ONLY with secondary encoding. A
  normal-vision floor below 15 is a hard FAIL - full-color readers can't tell the
  pair apart; re-step it on the adjacent pairlist (secondary encoding does not excuse
  this one); under `--pairs all` cut series or facet instead - see check 4. A contrast WARN
  obligates visible labels or a table view - it is not dismissable.
- **Thin marks; a legend always present for >= 2 series (none for one), with
  selective direct labels (never a number on every point); recessive grid/axes.**
- **Text wears text tokens, never the series color** - values, labels, and legends
  stay in primary/secondary/muted ink; a colored mark beside them carries identity.
- **Status colors are reserved** (good/warning/serious/critical) and never reused
  for "series 4"; they ship with an icon + label, never color alone.

## Plugging in a design system

The method is invariant; only these parameters change per system. The reference
instance - every value filled in - is `references/palette.md`.

| Parameter | What the system provides |
|---|---|
| **Ramps** | the hue scales (named steps) the palette draws from |
| **Categorical theme** | the fixed hue order (a named theme); default + alternates |
| **Sequential hue** | the default single hue for magnitude |
| **Diverging pair** | two warm/cool poles + a neutral midpoint |
| **Status palette** | good / warning / serious / critical - steps distinct from categorical |
| **Texture fill** | one directional hand-drawn fill, used at 45° / 135° |
| **Surfaces** | light & dark chart-surface colors (the validator needs these) |
| **Filter controls** | date-range & dimension controls (behavioral spec in `interaction.md`) |

To onboard a new system: fill those rows, feed its ramps to the validator, and let
it snap each slot to the nearest passing step. Structure and rules stay as written.

"""Estimate elastic modulus for each material from tensile test data.

Fits stress = E * strain + b by ordinary least squares, both per specimen
and pooled per material, then plots the data with the pooled fits.
"""

import json
import os

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

MATERIALS = ["aluminum", "steel", "titanium"]
# Fixed categorical order (first three slots validate all-pairs for CVD)
COLORS = {"aluminum": "#2a78d6", "steel": "#eb6834", "titanium": "#1baf7a"}
MARKERS = {"aluminum": "o", "steel": "s", "titanium": "^"}


def fit(strain, stress):
    """Return slope, intercept, and R^2 of a linear least-squares fit."""
    slope, intercept = np.polyfit(strain, stress, 1)
    pred = slope * strain + intercept
    ss_res = np.sum((stress - pred) ** 2)
    ss_tot = np.sum((stress - np.mean(stress)) ** 2)
    return slope, intercept, 1 - ss_res / ss_tot


df = pd.read_csv("measurements.csv")

# Per-specimen fits
rows = []
for (material, specimen), g in df.groupby(["material", "specimen"]):
    slope, intercept, r2 = fit(g["strain"].values, g["stress_mpa"].values)
    rows.append(
        {
            "material": material,
            "specimen": specimen,
            "modulus_gpa": slope / 1000,
            "intercept_mpa": intercept,
            "r2": r2,
        }
    )
specimens = pd.DataFrame(rows)

# Pooled fits per material, plus spread across specimens
summary = []
pooled = {}
for material in MATERIALS:
    g = df[df["material"] == material]
    slope, intercept, r2 = fit(g["strain"].values, g["stress_mpa"].values)
    pooled[material] = (slope, intercept)
    s = specimens[specimens["material"] == material]["modulus_gpa"]
    summary.append(
        {
            "material": material,
            "n_specimens": len(s),
            "modulus_pooled_gpa": slope / 1000,
            "intercept_pooled_mpa": intercept,
            "r2_pooled": r2,
            "modulus_specimen_mean_gpa": s.mean(),
            "modulus_specimen_std_gpa": s.std(ddof=1),
        }
    )
summary = pd.DataFrame(summary)

os.makedirs("results", exist_ok=True)
specimens.round(4).to_csv("results/specimen-moduli.csv", index=False)
summary.round(4).to_csv("results/moduli.csv", index=False)
with open("results/moduli.json", "w") as f:
    json.dump(summary.round(4).to_dict(orient="records"), f, indent=2)

# Figure: data points per specimen, pooled fit line per material
os.makedirs("figures", exist_ok=True)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 4.5), dpi=150)
strain_line = np.linspace(0, df["strain"].max() * 1.02, 50)
for material in MATERIALS:
    g = df[df["material"] == material]
    color = COLORS[material]
    ax.plot(
        g["strain"] * 100,
        g["stress_mpa"],
        linestyle="none",
        marker=MARKERS[material],
        markersize=5,
        markerfacecolor=color,
        markeredgecolor="white",
        markeredgewidth=0.8,
        alpha=0.85,
    )
    slope, intercept = pooled[material]
    E = slope / 1000
    ax.plot(
        strain_line * 100,
        slope * strain_line + intercept,
        color=color,
        linewidth=2,
        label=f"{material.capitalize()} (E = {E:.1f} GPa)",

# Elastic modulus from tensile test data

## Data and method

`measurements.csv` contains stress–strain data for three specimens each of
aluminum, steel, and titanium. Each specimen has 10 points spanning
0.02–0.20 % strain. All points appear to lie in the linear elastic region:
there is no sign of yield or curvature.

The elastic modulus *E* is the slope of an ordinary least-squares fit of
stress = *E* · strain + *b*:

- **Per specimen**: one fit per specimen, giving three estimates of *E* per
  material. The 95 % confidence interval on the mean uses a Student's
  *t*-distribution with 2 degrees of freedom.
- **Pooled**: one fit to all of a material's points. This is the line shown in
  the figure.

Every specimen was sampled at the same strain values, so the pooled slope is
exactly equal to the mean of the per-specimen slopes.

## Results

| Material | *E* (GPa) | Std. dev. across specimens (GPa) | 95 % CI (GPa) | Pooled R² | Typical handbook value (GPa) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Aluminum | 69.4 | 1.8 | ± 4.4 | 0.998 | ~69–70 |
| Steel | 199.1 | 2.0 | ± 5.0 | 0.998 | ~200–210 |
| Titanium | 116.6 | 1.7 | ± 4.2 | 0.998 | ~105–120 (Ti-6Al-4V ~114) |

![Stress vs. strain with linear fits](figures/stress-strain.png)

Per-specimen estimates (GPa):

| Aluminum | Steel | Titanium |
|---|---|---|
| AL-1: 70.1 | ST-1: 201.2 | TI-1: 114.6 |
| AL-2: 67.4 | ST-2: 197.3 | TI-2: 117.8 |
| AL-3: 70.6 | ST-3: 198.7 | TI-3: 117.2 |

## Discussion

- All three materials are fit very well by a straight line (R² ≥ 0.998 for
  every specimen). The fitted intercepts are within ±2.2 MPa of zero, which
  suggests no significant preload or zero offset.
- The moduli fall in the order steel > titanium > aluminum, with ratios of
  roughly 2.9 : 1.7 : 1. All three estimates agree with typical handbook
  values for these material classes.
- Specimens of the same material differ by about 2–3 % (coefficient of
  variation ≈ 1.5–2.5 %). The confidence intervals are wide relative to that
  scatter because there are only three specimens per material.
- The scatter is mostly point-to-point noise rather than a systematic trend.
  The noise grows with stress (see steel at 0.2 % strain), which is consistent
  with error proportional to load. A weighted fit would give slightly tighter
  estimates, but the conclusions would be the same.

## Reproducing

This is a [Calkit](https://calkit.org) project. Running `calkit run` executes
the `analyze` pipeline stage (`scripts/analyze.py`) in the `main` uv
environment. The stage regenerates:

- `results/moduli.csv` / `results/moduli.json`: per-material summary
- `results/specimen-moduli.csv`: per-specimen fits
- `figures/stress-strain.png`: the figure above

# Elastic modulus from tensile test data

## Data and method

`measurements.csv` contains stress–strain data for three specimens each of
aluminum, steel, and titanium. Each specimen has 10 points spanning
0.02–0.20 % strain. All points appear to lie in the linear elastic region:
there is no sign of yield or curvature.

The elastic modulus *E* is the slope of an ordinary least-squares fit of
stress = *E* · strain + *b*:

- **Per specimen**: one fit per specimen, giving three estimates of *E* per
  material. The 95 % confidence interval on the mean uses a Student's
  *t*-distribution with 2 degrees of freedom.
- **Pooled**: one fit to all of a material's points. This is the line shown in
  the figure.

Every specimen was sampled at the same strain values, so the pooled slope is
exactly equal to the mean of the per-specimen slopes.

## Results

| Material | *E* (GPa) | Std. dev. across specimens (GPa) | 95 % CI (GPa) | Pooled R² | Typical handbook value (GPa) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Aluminum | 69.4 | 1.8 | ± 4.4 | 0.998 | ~69–70 |
| Steel | 199.1 | 2.0 | ± 5.0 | 0.998 | ~200–210 |
| Titanium | 116.6 | 1.7 | ± 4.2 | 0.998 | ~105–120 (Ti-6Al-4V ~114) |

| Aluminum | Steel | Titanium |

| AL-3: 70.6 | ST-3: 198.7 | TI-3: 117.2 |

  every specimen). The fitted intercepts are within ±2.2 MPa of zero, which
  suggests no significant preload or zero offset.

  roughly 2.9 : 1.7 : 1. All three estimates agree with typical handbook

  variation ≈ 1.5–2.5 %). The confidence intervals are wide relative to that

- The scatter is mostly point-to-point noise rather than a systematic trend.

  with error proportional to load. A weighted fit would give slightly tighter
  estimates, but the conclusions would be the same.

I set the folder up as a Calkit project and estimated the elastic modulus of all three materials. Every specimen fits a straight line closely, and all three values are in line with typical handbook values.

| Material | E (GPa) | 95% CI | R² | Handbook |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Steel | 199.1 | ± 5.0 | 0.998 | ~200–210 |
| Titanium | 116.6 | ± 4.2 | 0.998 | ~105–120 |
| Aluminum | 69.4 | ± 4.4 | 0.998 | ~69–70 |

- **Method:** each modulus is the slope of a least-squares fit of stress against strain. I fit each specimen separately to get the spread and confidence interval, and also fit all of a material's points together for the line in the figure. The two give the same slope here because every specimen was measured at the same strain values.
- **Linear region:** all points look like they're within the elastic range (no sign of yield), and the fitted intercepts are all within about ±2 MPa of zero.
- **Spread:** specimens of the same material differ by 2–5% from lowest to highest. The confidence intervals are wide compared with that because there are only three specimens per material.
- **Noise:** the scatter gets larger at higher stress (visible on steel at 0.2% strain). A weighted fit would tighten the estimates slightly but wouldn't change the conclusions.

The handbook column is from general knowledge, not your data.

**What's in the project:**
- `scripts/analyze.py` does the fits and makes the figure. Calkit runs it as a pipeline step called `analyze` in a Python environment I set up (numpy, pandas, matplotlib, scipy).
- `results/moduli.csv` and `results/moduli.json` hold the per-material summary; `results/specimen-moduli.csv` has the per-specimen fits.
- `figures/stress-strain.png` shows the data points and fit lines for each material, with the modulus labelled on each line. It's registered as a Calkit figure.
- `report.md` is the write-up: method, results tables, the figure and discussion.

Running `calkit run` regenerates everything if the data changes, and `calkit status` shows the pipeline is up to date. Your `measurements.csv` is still at the top level.

**Things to know:**
- I created a Git repository and made a few commits. Nothing has been pushed anywhere.
- The figure is stored with DVC, which Calkit uses for files like images, rather than directly in Git. No remote storage is configured, so if you want to share the project you'll need to add one or tell Calkit to keep the image in Git.
- I wrote `report.md` by hand from the results, so if the data changes, its numbers won't update when you re-run the pipeline.
